_comment: Guided tour for 2D-FLCS. The UI is a declarative AutoForm view (flc_2d.view.json), so most steps target bound attributes; the toolbar is QActions, reached by {'action': ...}. The tour walks on the plugin's OWN simulator, whose answer is known (tau 1/3 ns, k12=30, k21=10 -> 25 ms relaxation, 0.25/0.75 populations), so it needs no data of the user's. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: Two lifetimes, and whether a molecule changed between them
steps.text:
Ordinary FCS correlates total intensity, so two species that diffuse alike are one curve. Filtered FCS can separate them — but only if you already know their decay patterns.

2D-FLCS drops that requirement. At a chosen lag it measures the joint distribution of the first photon's micro-time and the second photon's, then inverts it into a map over pairs of lifetimes. Nothing is known in advance; no second colour, detector or polarisation.

Eight steps, walked on a stream this tool simulates itself.

steps.title: The answer, before you press anything
steps.text:
These fields drive a two-state exchange simulator, so the tour can run with no data of yours — and you can check the result, because you set it.

With the defaults τ₁ = 1 ns, τ₂ = 3 ns, k₁₂ = 30 s⁻¹, k₂₁ = 10 s⁻¹, two numbers are fixed:
• equilibrium populations 0.25 / 0.75, from p₁ = k₂₁/(k₁₂+k₂₁);
• relaxation time 1/(k₁₂+k₂₁) = 25 ms.

Remember the 25 ms. The next step is about it.

steps.title: Simulate the stream
steps.text: Sim generates the photon stream and loads it as the active dataset; the status bar reports how many photons and with which parameters. On a real measurement this is where Open would go instead.

await.hint: Press Sim to generate the demo stream.

steps.title: The lag is the question you are asking
steps.text:
lag selects which photon pairs are histogrammed, and win is its half-width.

The default lag is 1 ms — one twenty-fifth of the 25 ms exchange time you just set. Almost nothing has interconverted in that time, so the map should come out nearly pure diagonal. That is not a failure; it is the right answer to the question you asked.

Raise the lag toward 25 ms and the cross-peaks appear. A single lag never answers a question about kinetics — build the map at several and watch them grow.

A wider window buys photon pairs at the cost of lag resolution. On real data that trade is usually worth taking: the map starves of pairs long before it starves of resolution.

steps.title: The inversion is ill-posed, and that is the whole difficulty
steps.text:
Recovering lifetimes from a decay is an inverse Laplace transform: many quite different distributions fit about equally well, and noise picks between them.

Tikhonov is closed-form and fastest; NNLS enforces non-negativity and is the default; MEM is the most faithful to what the data actually support — it will not sharpen a peak the data do not justify — and the slowest.

Leave log λ at 0 and the regularisation is chosen from the L-curve: residual against solution norm, take the corner. Look at that panel afterwards. No clear corner means the data do not determine the answer, and a hand-picked λ is then your decision, not theirs.

One consequence worth carrying: a regularised inversion controls how sharp a peak may be, so peak width reports the regularisation, not the sample. Read positions and areas.

steps.title: Below a nanosecond you are fitting the instrument
steps.text:
A wrong IRF does not give you a bad fit. It gives you a good fit to the wrong lifetime.

Synthetic builds a Gaussian pulse from the centre, FWHM and skew below; Detect places one at the decay's own prompt rise; File uses a measured IRF loaded with the IRF button; None tail-fits without one — honest only when every lifetime of interest is far longer than the pulse.

The rise toggle scans the IRF position during the 1D-MEM and averages around the optimum: a little resolution for a much smaller timing systematic.

steps.title: Run it
steps.text: The 2D decay-correlation matrix is built at the chosen lag, rebinned, and inverted into the lifetime–lifetime map. With corr enabled the species-filtered correlations and the interconversion rates follow.

steps.title: Read off the diagonal, then check three things
steps.text:
Diagonal peaks are species that still had the same lifetime one lag later — static heterogeneity. Off-diagonal peaks are molecules that changed state during the lag. The diagonal is essentially the ordinary lifetime distribution; the information that is only here is off it.

Then, before believing any of it:
1. The 2D residual must be structureless noise. Structure there means the model did not describe the data, and every peak position is suspect.
2. The species correlation is the real cross-check. Two exchanging states must show the autocorrelations decaying and the cross-correlation anti-correlated, both at k = k₁₂ + k₂₁. If they do not, the peaks are not two exchanging states.
3. Equal-brightness states are ill-conditioned. The inversion separates by decay shape, so two states of the same brightness and similar lifetime are nearly degenerate — which is why the global multi-lag MEM is marked advanced.

The ? button has the rest.
